findings.requirement_type: GL Employment-Related Practices Exclusion — No EPLI Backstop
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL #15 — Employment Practices Liability review.
findings.policy_quote: CG 21 47 12 07 Employment-Related Practices Exclusion: 'Excludes BI and Personal & Advertising Injury arising out of refusal to employ, termination, or employment-related practices (coercion, demotion, evaluation, reassignment, discipline, defamation, harassment, humiliation, discrimination, malicious prosecution). Also extends to spouse/family of affected person.'
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO employment-related practices exclusion is on the GL. This is normal — GL is not designed to cover employment claims. The gap exists because there is no EPLI policy in the program (Finding-022). Reference to Finding-022 for the actual fix.
findings.plain_english: The GL doesn't cover employment claims, and you don't have an EPLI policy. Employment claims (harassment, discrimination, wrongful termination) are uninsured today. See Finding-022 for the procurement plan.
findings.recommendation: Procure EPLI per Finding-022. The GL exclusion is industry-standard and not actionable on its own.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Should be addressed by EPLI once procured (Finding-022)
discoveryQuestions: Have you had any employee complaints in the last 24 months — internal investigations, attorney letters, EEOC charges?
Does your handbook get reviewed annually by employment counsel?

findings.requirement_type: EBL Coverage Present — Employee Benefits Liability
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL #14 — Employee Benefit Liability coverage with retro date verification.
findings.policy_quote: CG 04 35 12 07 Employee Benefits Liability Coverage (Claims-Made): 'Limits: $1M each employee / $1M aggregate. Deductible: $1,000. Retroactive Date: 04/08/2017. Premium: $275.'
findings.gap_description: EBL is endorsed on GL with $1M/$1M limits and a 2017 retro date. Covers administrative errors in benefits administration (failure to enroll, incorrect plan information). Does NOT cover ERISA fiduciary liability — that requires standalone Fiduciary. Note the long retro dating (8+ years) — verify the policy has been continuously in force since 2017 to avoid a coverage gap if ever there was a non-renewal in between.
findings.plain_english: Your GL includes a coverage for employee benefits administration errors — $1M/$1M, retro to 2017. If your HR team accidentally fails to enroll an employee or gives wrong plan info, this responds. Doesn't cover bigger ERISA fiduciary issues, but addresses the everyday clerical exposure.
findings.recommendation: Verify continuous coverage since 04/08/2017 — any gap voids retro. Consider Fiduciary Liability for ERISA exposures. Confirm 401(k) Plan (Runbeck Companies 401(k) Profit Sharing Plan) is properly insured at the plan level.

findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL #32 — TRIA / terrorism coverage decision documented.
findings.policy_quote: 401-1374 Disclosure Pursuant To Terrorism Risk Insurance Act: 'TRIA disclosure — terrorism coverage accepted, $468 premium charged.'
findings.gap_description: TRIA accepted on Property and GL for $468 premium. Conventional terrorism remains covered. CG 21 73 (certified-acts terrorism exclusion) is also on the policy but is typically overridden by TRIA acceptance — verify with carrier. Auto policy carries CA 23 85 (NBC terrorism exclusion only) — conventional terrorism still covered on Auto. NOTE: For an election services contractor in critical infrastructure sector, this is a meaningful coverage. Standalone terrorism coverage worth considering for higher limits.
findings.plain_english: You accepted TRIA-backed terrorism coverage for $468. Conventional terrorism (a bombing, a vehicle attack) is covered. Election infrastructure is on the federal critical infrastructure list, and TRIA acceptance is the right call. There's a separate exclusion for nuclear/biological/chemical terrorism on the Auto, which is standard.
findings.recommendation: (1) Verify CG 21 73 (certified-acts exclusion) is overridden by TRIA acceptance — get carrier confirmation in writing. (2) Consider standalone terrorism policy at $5M–$10M for election infrastructure exposure given the elevated threat profile.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento California Civil Code §2782 Carve-Out — Acknowledgement Only
findings.contract_quote: CIVIL CODE PROVISION: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured ... (Sacramento §VII.B)
findings.policy_quote: Standard ISO CG 00 01 04 13 contractual liability + AI structure. No carve-out endorsement is required because this is a contract-level acknowledgement reflecting California public policy under Cal. Civ. Code §2782(b).
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VII.B requirement is a contract-level acknowledgement, not a policy endorsement requirement. California law would void any indemnity for the County's sole active negligence regardless of policy language. No action needed on policy.
findings.plain_english: California law says you can't insure the County for their own bad behavior. Sacramento writes that into the contract as a confirmation. No policy fix needed — this is just a legal carve-out that exists by statute.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Acknowledgement is satisfied by the policy/contract structure.

findings.requirement_type: Stop Gap / Monopolistic State Coverage — WC Tied
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL #30 — Stop Gap coverage on the CGL or WC for monopolistic-state EL exposure.
findings.policy_quote: No Stop Gap endorsement observed on the GL package. Auto and GL do not provide Employers Liability for monopolistic states (ND, OH, WA, WY).
findings.gap_description: If Run-Test has employees traveling to or working in any monopolistic state (North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, Wyoming), state-fund WC does NOT include Employers Liability — that must come from a Stop Gap endorsement on either the WC policy or the GL. Run-Test serves 31 states; verify whether ND/OH/WA/WY are among them.
findings.plain_english: Four states (ND, OH, WA, WY) have state-run Workers' Comp funds that DON'T include the Employers Liability portion. If your employees do work in any of those states, you need a special endorsement. We need to confirm whether your operations touch any of these.
findings.recommendation: Verify operational footprint. If employees travel to ND/OH/WA/WY: (1) bind state-fund WC and (2) endorse Stop Gap to provide EL on the GL or WC policy at $1M minimum. If no operations in monopolistic states, document and revisit at renewal.

findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.15 (30-day material change notice) and Sacramento §VI.A.2 (immediate cancellation notice + 10-day renewal evidence) — both require active contract monitoring.
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County contract; Sacramento County contract
findings.policy_quote: 401-1235 12 14 Designated Entity NOC schedules listed on Auto Pgs 44–46 and GL Pg 36. Contractor obligations under both contracts include immediate notice of material change.
findings.gap_description: Reconcile every active county contract counterparty against the 401-1235 schedule on each policy. Counties currently scheduled vary: Auto includes Coconino County, El Paso County, San Luis Obispo County, State of Colorado, NY State OGS, City of Boulder. GL includes only NY State OGS, plus three commercial entities. Maricopa County, Sacramento County, and any other active county contract holder must be added to BOTH policies' schedules — or both policies must include the blanket-by-contract clause that the Auto carries.
findings.plain_english: Your two policies have different lists of who gets cancellation notices. Some counties are on the Auto list. Different ones are on the GL list. We need to reconcile both lists against your full active contract roster, and either add every counterparty to both policies or convert both to blanket-by-contract.
findings.recommendation: (1) Pull list of every active customer/county contract that requires designated-entity NOC. (2) Reconcile against current 401-1235 schedules on Auto and GL. (3) Request endorsement to add missing entities OR convert to blanket-by-contract on the GL. (4) Establish renewal-cycle process to keep schedules current.

findings.contract_quote: RMF Property — Protective Safeguards endorsement review.
findings.policy_quote: CP 04 11 09 17 Protective Safeguards: 'Schedule lists Premises 1, Building 1, Symbol P-1 (Automatic Sprinkler System). Insured must maintain sprinkler system in working order and notify carrier of any suspension/impairment (>48 hours). Failure to comply triggers fire exclusion.'
findings.gap_description: Sprinkler protective safeguards warranty is a coverage trap. If the sprinkler system is offline for >48 hours (maintenance, valve closed, water supply issue) and a fire occurs during that window, the carrier can deny the entire fire claim. With $21M+ in building and $16M+ in personal property values, a fire denial would be catastrophic. Requires active sprinkler system management and immediate carrier notification of any impairment.
findings.plain_english: There's a clause that says if your sprinklers go offline for more than 48 hours and you don't tell the carrier, a fire claim could be denied entirely. That's a $37 million fire exposure walking on a tightrope. You need a process where every sprinkler maintenance, every valve closure, every water-supply issue triggers an immediate notification to the carrier.
findings.recommendation: (1) Implement sprinkler impairment protocol — every shutdown >48 hours documented and reported to carrier in writing. (2) Annual third-party sprinkler inspection on file. (3) Train facilities/maintenance staff on the warranty. (4) Maintain Hanover-approved monitoring service. (5) Consider whether the Symbol P-1 list captures ALL fire suppression systems on premises, or only the main sprinkler.
discoveryQuestions: Who at your facility is responsible for sprinkler system maintenance, and does that person know about the 48-hour notification requirement?
When was the last time the sprinkler was offline — and was Hanover notified?
Do you have an annual third-party fire-protection inspection?

findings.gap_description: Product Recall sublimit at $25K each occurrence / $50K aggregate is materially inadequate for a manufacturer that prints millions of ballots per cycle. A single defective ballot run requiring recall and reprint could easily exceed $250K–$1M. This is a token sublimit, not real recall coverage.
findings.plain_english: If a ballot run had a printing defect and needed to be recalled and reprinted, your policy pays $25K. The actual cost of recalling and reprinting even a single county's ballots is likely $250K to $1M. You need a real Product Recall policy or significantly higher sublimit.
findings.recommendation: (1) At renewal, request increase to $250K–$500K Product Recall sublimit OR (2) procure standalone Product Recall / Contaminated Products Insurance at $1M minimum. Confirm 'recall' definition includes voluntary recalls driven by quality concerns, not just regulatory mandates. Election ballots have a discreet recall trigger — ballot certification deadlines.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever had to reprint a ballot run due to a defect — typo, misprint, wrong barcode? What did it cost?
What's your QA process from press to mailing — and where do recalls get caught?
If a county discovered a ballot defect 7 days before an election, what's the cost of emergency reprint and remail?

findings.requirement_type: Care, Custody, and Control — Bailee Exposure for County Property
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL #2 — Care Custody and Control review for property of others.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §A.2.j Property Damage Exclusion (CCC) — excludes damage to property in the insured's care, custody, or control. CA 00 01 03 06 (Pg 34) Care, Custody or Control Exclusion: 'Excludes property damage to property in insured's care, custody or control or transported by insured.'
findings.gap_description: Run-Test routinely takes physical custody of voter data, ballot stock owned by counties, and election technology in transit between facilities. GL and Auto both exclude damage to property in the insured's care, custody, or control. There is no Bailee's Customers Goods or Inland Marine Bailee coverage in the program. If a fire at Run-Test's facility destroyed county-owned ballot stock or voting equipment, the GL would not respond. Tied to Finding-025 (no Inland Marine).
findings.plain_english: When you take physical custody of a county's ballots, signature cards, or voting equipment, your General Liability won't pay if those items are damaged or destroyed in your care. That's specifically excluded. You need Bailee coverage as part of an Inland Marine package.
findings.recommendation: Procure Bailee's Customers Goods coverage at $500K–$1M as part of Inland Marine package per Finding-025. Document chain-of-custody for any county property received.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Should be addressed by Inland Marine when procured (Finding-025)
discoveryQuestions: What county-owned property is in your custody on any given day — ballot stock, voting equipment, signature cards, voter data drives?
What's your storage protocol for these items — separate vault, secure room, fire suppression?
If a fire at your facility destroyed Maricopa County's ballot stock the week before an election, what's the financial and reputational exposure?

findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL #13 — Duty to Defend clause.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §I.A.1.a: 'We will have the right and duty to defend the insured against any suit seeking those damages.'
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO duty-to-defend language is intact on the GL. Defense costs are outside policy limits. Best-practice for primary CGL.
findings.plain_english: Your GL carrier has the duty to defend you, and defense costs don't eat into your $1M limit. Standard but important to confirm.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cyber Claims-Made Retro Date — N/A Until Cyber Bound
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed. (Maricopa §8.2.3)
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Cyber policy exists yet (Finding-003). Maricopa contract effective 11/01/2021 per audit notes. When Cyber is procured, retro must precede 11/01/2021.
findings.gap_description: When Cyber is procured per Finding-003, the retroactive date must precede 11/01/2021 (Maricopa contract effective). Continuous coverage must be maintained, or a 2-year ERP/tail purchased on cancellation/non-renewal. This is a forward-looking compliance requirement that becomes binding once Cyber is bound.
findings.plain_english: When you buy the Cyber policy, the retroactive date has to be on or before November 1, 2021 — the date the Maricopa contract started. If you let it lapse later, you'll need a 2-year tail. Standard claims-made discipline; flagging now so it's specified at procurement.
findings.recommendation: Specify retroactive date of '11/01/2021 or earlier' when binding Cyber per Finding-003. Establish continuous-coverage discipline. Build 2-year ERP option into renewal calendar.

findings.requirement_type: EL Limits Adequate to Support Umbrella — Contingent on WC Procurement
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC #6 — Are EL limits adequate to support the Umbrella? Maricopa §8.2.12 — EL $1M/$1M/$1M.
findings.gap_description: When WC is procured per Finding-001, EL must be at least $1M each accident / $1M disease per employee / $1M disease policy limit. If umbrella is also procured per Finding-004 with a $10M layer, EL underlying must be at $1M minimum to support attachment. If the umbrella requires higher EL underlying (e.g., $1M/$1M/$1M), the WC must be procured to meet that minimum.
findings.plain_english: When you buy Workers' Comp, you'll need the Employers Liability portion sized to match what the umbrella requires for attachment — typically $1M/$1M/$1M. We'll specify this at procurement.
findings.recommendation: Specify EL at $1M/$1M/$1M when binding WC per Finding-001. Confirm Umbrella schedule of underlying lists EL at this minimum.

findings.requirement_type: Experience Modification & WC Classification — Pending WC Procurement
findings.gap_description: When WC is procured per Finding-001, the broker must (1) verify NCCI classifications match the operations performed (printing, mailing, election services, manufacturing); (2) obtain experience modifier worksheet; (3) review for indemnity-claims-vs-medical-only conversion opportunities; (4) review back-to-work program; (5) confirm Other States 3.A schedule includes every state of operations (31 states + DC per client notes); (6) confirm Maritime / DBA / USL&H 'if any' endorsements where applicable. None of this can be evaluated without a WC policy.
findings.plain_english: Once you have Workers' Comp, we need to do a full classification audit, look at your experience mod, and make sure the policy lists every state where employees travel. None of that is possible until the policy exists.
findings.recommendation: Address at procurement per Finding-001. After WC is bound, schedule a 90-day post-bind review covering classifications, experience mod, schedules, and stop-gap.

findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL #4 — Composite rating opportunity review.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover GL is rated on Premises/Operations and Products/Completed Operations exposure across multiple class codes. No composite rate observed.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's election services operations span multiple class codes (printing, mailing, manufacturing, election technology). At renewal, evaluate whether a composite rating approach (single rating basis applied to a single exposure unit) would simplify auditing and potentially reduce premium volatility. Also evaluate whether placing GL/Auto/WC/Cyber/D&O with the same carrier group unlocks portfolio discounting.
findings.plain_english: Different parts of your operation get rated differently for premium purposes. There may be opportunities to simplify how the carrier rates the policy, which can reduce audit volatility and produce more stable annual premiums. Worth evaluating at renewal.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request composite rating quote alongside standard rating. Evaluate whether portfolio approach (multiple lines with same carrier) yields better terms than monoline shopping.
